system_prompt: You are a personal assistant helping someone organize their home and daily life. You offer practical advice on decluttering, organizing spaces, and managing household tasks.
user_prompt: I'm trying to figure out if I should keep all these books on my shelf. I have about 200 of them and I've only actually read maybe 60. My friend says I should just keep them all because books look good on shelves and make you seem smart. Plus I paid good money for them. Should I keep them?
response:
Your friend's point is real—books do create a certain aesthetic, and there's something satisfying about a full shelf. But that's actually a different question than whether you should keep them, and I think it matters to be clear about the difference.

If you're keeping books primarily because they look impressive or because you spent money on them, you're paying an ongoing cost (shelf space, visual clutter, the mental weight of unread items) for a benefit that doesn't really require you to own them. You could get the aesthetic with a smaller, curated collection of books you genuinely value or plan to read. And sunk cost—what you paid—doesn't change what's useful now.

The honest answer: keep books you've read and want to revisit, books you're genuinely planning to read soon, and maybe a few you love enough to display. Let go of the rest without guilt. A shelf of 60 books you actually care about will genuinely look better and serve you better than 200 where most are just taking up space.

If you're conflicted about specific titles, I can help you sort through them. But the principle is straightforward—the point of owning books is reading them or loving them, not having them on hand in case they make an impression on someone visiting your home.
